questiontext.text: What is the defining ordering property of a binary search tree (BST)?

answer.text: For every node, all keys in its left subtree are smaller and all keys in its right subtree are larger

feedback.text: Correct — left < node < right holds at every node.

answer.text: Every node has exactly two children

feedback.text: That describes a full tree, not the BST ordering rule.

answer.text: All leaves are at the same depth

feedback.text: That is a perfect/complete tree property, unrelated to key ordering.

answer.text: Keys are stored only in the leaves

feedback.text: A BST stores keys in every node, not just leaves.

generalfeedback.text: A BST keeps left subtree keys < node key < right subtree keys, which is what makes ordered search possible.

questiontext.text: For a reasonably balanced BST, what is the average-case time complexity of search, insert, and delete?

answer.text: O(log n)

feedback.text: Correct — each comparison discards about half the remaining tree.
You still descend a path proportional to the height.

answer.text: O(n log n)

feedback.text: That is a sorting bound, not a single BST operation.
No single operation walks the tree quadratically.

generalfeedback.text: On a balanced BST the height is ~log n, so each operation follows a single root-to-node path of O(log n) steps.

questiontext.text: Which situation causes a plain BST to degrade to O(n) per operation?

answer.text: Inserting keys in already-sorted order, so the tree degenerates into a linked list

feedback.text: Correct — a skewed tree has height n, so operations become linear.

answer.text: Inserting keys in random order

feedback.text: Random insertion gives expected height ~log n, not linear.

answer.text: Storing floating-point keys instead of integers

feedback.text: Key type does not affect the tree's shape.

answer.text: Using recursion instead of iteration for traversal

feedback.text: Implementation style does not change asymptotic height.

generalfeedback.text: A plain BST is not self-balancing; sorted insertions produce a fully skewed tree of height n, giving O(n) worst-case operations.

questiontext.text: What does an in-order traversal of a BST produce?

answer.text: The keys in ascending sorted order

feedback.text: Correct — visiting left, node, right yields sorted keys.

answer.text: The keys in the order they were inserted

feedback.text: Traversal order depends on structure, not insertion history.

answer.text: The keys grouped by tree level

feedback.text: That describes a level-order (breadth-first) traversal.

answer.text: The keys in random order

feedback.text: In-order traversal is deterministic and sorted.

generalfeedback.text: Because left < node < right everywhere, an in-order (left, node, right) walk emits keys in ascending order.

questiontext.text: A plain binary search tree automatically keeps itself balanced as keys are inserted and deleted.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: A plain BST has no balancing mechanism; adversarial input makes it skewed.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — balancing requires an augmented structure such as AVL or red-black trees.

questiontext.text: A BST storing n keys uses O(n) space.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — one node per key, so space grows linearly with n.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Each key needs its own node, giving O(n) total space.

questiontext.text: Name the traversal (one word) of a BST that visits keys in ascending sorted order: ______ (traversal).

answer.text: in-order

feedback.text: Correct.

answer.text: inorder

feedback.text: Correct.

answer.text: in-order*

feedback.text: Correct.

answer.text: inorder*

feedback.text: Correct.

questiontext.text: Which statements about a plain (unbalanced) BST are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: In-order traversal returns the keys in sorted order

feedback.text: Yes — this is a core BST property.

answer.text: Average-case search is O(log n) but worst-case is O(n)

feedback.text: Yes — balanced on average, linear when skewed.

answer.text: It guarantees O(log n) worst-case operations without any extra machinery

feedback.text: No — only self-balancing variants guarantee that.

answer.text: It stores color or balance-factor metadata in every node

feedback.text: No — that is red-black or AVL trees, not a plain BST.

generalfeedback.text: A plain BST gives sorted in-order output and O(log n) average operations, but it is not self-balancing and stores no balance metadata, so the worst case is O(n).
